question.prompt: The vertices of an equilateral triangle lie on the hyperbola \(xy=1,\) and a vertex of this hyperbola is the centroid of the triangle. What is the square of the area of the triangle?

solutions.title: Use symmetry and the centroid
solutions.explanation:
In an equilateral triangle, the medians are also perpendicular bisectors, so the centroid is equally distant from all three vertices. This connects the triangle to the symmetry of \(xy=1\).

The hyperbola has vertices \((1,1)\) and \((-1,-1)\). A half-turn about the origin preserves the hyperbola and all areas, so assume the triangle's centroid is \(G=(1,1)\). Name its vertices \(P,Q,R\), choosing \(P,Q\) on the same branch. Such a pair exists because the hyperbola has only two branches.

For a point \((x,y)\) on the hyperbola, put \(u=x+y\). Since \(xy=1\), its squared distance from \(G\) is
\[
(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=u^2-2u.
\]
Also, \(u^2=(x-y)^2+4\ge4\). Thus coordinate sums on the first-quadrant branch are at least \(2\), and those on the third-quadrant branch are at most \(-2\).

Let the coordinate sums of \(P,Q\) be \(u,v\). Because \(GP=GQ\),
\[
0=(u^2-2u)-(v^2-2v)=(u-v)(u+v-2).
\]
The same-branch condition makes \(u+v-2\) nonzero, so \(u=v\). Both coordinate pairs therefore have sum \(u\) and product \(1\), meaning their coordinates are roots of the same quadratic \(t^2-ut+1=0\). Since the points are distinct, they have the form \(P=(a,b)\), \(Q=(b,a)\), with \(a\ne b\).

The midpoint of \(PQ\) lies on \(y=x\), and \(PQ\) is perpendicular to that line. Hence \(y=x\) is its perpendicular bisector. Since \(RP=RQ\), the third vertex \(R\) lies there too. Its only possible locations on the hyperbola are \((1,1)\) and \((-1,-1)\). The centroid cannot be a triangle vertex, so \(R=(-1,-1)\).

Consequently,
\[
GR=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2.
\]
The centroid lies two-thirds of the way along a median from its vertex. Since that median is also an altitude, the altitude is
\[
h=\frac32GR=3\sqrt2.
\]
For an equilateral triangle of side length \(s\), \(h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s\), giving \(s=2\sqrt6\). Its area is
\[
K=\frac12sh=\frac12(2\sqrt6)(3\sqrt2)=6\sqrt3.
\]
Therefore \(K^2=\boxed{108}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
